---
title: "Flow Matching"
---
The flow matching transformer model is a flexible and stochastic surrogate.


## When this might be a good fit

The flow matching surrogate is a good option when stochasticity is needed. Architecturally, it is implemented as a modified transformer and also supports static and sequence conditioning. 

## How flow matching works

### Architecture
The flow matching surrogate is parametrised with a *non-causal* transformer that processes the entire sequence in parallel.

### Flow Matching

Flow Matching and Diffusion models are the current state-of-the-art learning algorithms for continuous valued data (e.g. images, protein-structure prediction). In brief, these models learn time-varying velocity fields which can be used to transport a sample of pure noise (e.g. from a Gaussian) to the data distribution. In order to generate samples the time-varying velocity field $v_{\theta}$ must be integrated over time $t$ to transport a noise sample $x_0$ to the data distribution:
$$
x_{\mathrm{pred}} = x_0+\int_{t=0}^{t=1}v_{\theta}(x_t|c)dt\text{, where } c \text{ is conditioning (i.e. surrogate inputs)}
$$


In practice this is achieved via numerical ODE solvers like Euler or Heun, with the number of solver steps introducing a trade-off between speed and quality.

:::{.callout-note  title="Technical note" collapse="true"}
Diffusion models have equivalent ODE and SDE forms and can be sampled via SDE-solvers like Euler-Maruyama or ODE-solvers like Heun. See @song2021scorebased.
:::

By fixing the conditioning $c$ and varying the initial noise, you can sample multiple realisations rather than the average realisation that an MLP or Autoregressive transformer learn.

:::{.callout-tip}
The mathematical details of these models and the derivation of their training objectives are out of scope but if you're interested you may find these resources helpful:

* [Accessible introduction to Diffusion (YouTube)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iv-5mZ_9CPY)
* [Introduction to Normalising Flows and Flow Matching (Blog)](https://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/blog/2024/01/20/flow-matching.html)
* [Explanation of score-based diffusion by its inventor (Blog)](https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/#connection-to-diffusion-models-and-others)
* [Unifying flow matching and diffusion (Monograph)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.21890)

:::


## Configuring a Flow Matching model

Metis uses Flow Matching with a fixed linear path from Gaussian noise $x_0$ to a training sequence $x_1$: $x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx_1$. The network learns the velocity target $x_1-x_0$ at uniformly sampled times $t\in[0,1]$.

Architecture and sampling settings share a single flat model config. For example, `configs/model/flow_matching_default.yaml` contains:

```yaml
defaults:
  - flow_matching_schema
  - _self_

num_steps: 50
solver: heun
multi_mode: median

n_blocks: 12
n_head: 8
n_kv_head: 8
qkv_bias: true
embd_dim: 64
cond_dropout_prob: 0.0
in_and_out_biases: true
cross_attn: null
```

The schema supplies `_target_: models.sit.create_flow_matching_transformer`. Select a preset with `model=flow_matching_default` and override fields directly, for example `model.n_blocks=8 model.num_steps=100`.

### Sampling settings

* `num_steps`: Number of ODE solver steps for evaluation and inference; does not affect training.
* `solver`: Either `heun` or `euler`. Euler is first-order; Heun uses a second-order correction on all but the final step, which uses Euler.
* `multi_mode`: Controls comparison-plot sampling during training. `median` uses the parameter-group median static inputs (and median observed sequences, when conditioning). `entire_param_group` generates a sample for each entry's static inputs. The latter is useful for models like HRP and Magenta where realisations within the same parameter group can have different static inputs; it currently does not support sequence conditioning.

### Architecture settings

* `sequence_len`: Number of timesteps in the data sequence.
* `data_dim`: Number of predicted variables per timestep.
* `cond_dim`: Number of static input variables.
* `n_blocks`: Number of transformer blocks.
* `n_head`: Number of query heads in attention layers.
* `n_kv_head`: Number of key-value heads in attention layers; must divide `n_head`.
* `qkv_bias`: Whether the query, key, and value projections in self-attention use biases.
* `embd_dim`: Hidden dimension of the network.
* `cond_dropout_prob`: Probability of replacing the static conditioning embedding with a fixed zero embedding during training. Defaults to zero. This is a building block for [classifier-free guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598), but guided sampling is not implemented.
* `in_and_out_biases`: Controls biases in the data input projection and the optional conditioning-sequence input projection. Despite the name, the final output projection always has a bias.
* `cross_attn`: Cross-attention configuration for sequence conditioning, or `null` for static-only conditioning. For example, add `+model/cross_attn=default` when the dataset specifies `observed_output_variables`.

Training derives `sequence_len`, `data_dim`, and `cond_dim` from the dataset config. With sequence conditioning, `data_dim` counts only predicted variables and `cross_attn.cond_dim` is set to the number of observed variables.


| Config | `n_blocks` | `n_head` | `n_kv_head` | `embd_dim` 
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `flow_matching_small` | 6 | 4 | 4 | 64 |
| `flow_matching_default` | 12 | 8 | 8 | 64 |
| `flow_matching_large` | 16 | 16 | 16 | 128 |
